lessons.title: Mapping AI to awareness, consideration, conversion and retention
lessons.body:
### Why think in funnels

It is tempting to use AI randomly, a caption here and an email there. You get far more value by mapping it to the stages customers move through. A simple funnel has four stages: **awareness** (they discover you), **consideration** (they evaluate you), **conversion** (they buy or book) and **retention** (they stay, return and refer).

### Awareness: getting discovered

AI helps you produce more relevant top-of-funnel content without burning out.

- **Content ideation:** "Give me 20 video ideas for first-time home buyers in Dubai, grouped by fear, dream and myth."
- **Hook variations:** multiple opening lines to test on short-form video.
- **Repurposing:** one long video into shorts, carousel slides, a newsletter and a thread.
- **Localization:** draft versions for different languages or regions, polished by native speakers.
- **Search and discovery:** outline articles around the questions your audience actually asks.

Human role: choose ideas that fit your brand and positioning, add real stories, and check trends are real and current.

### Consideration: building trust

People compare options, read reviews and look for proof.

- **FAQ and objection content:** summarize real customer questions from DMs and comments (anonymized), then draft answers.
- **Comparison and explainer content:** "Explain the difference between our two packages for a busy restaurant owner."
- **Case study drafts** from interview notes, with the client's approval of final wording.
- **Personalized outreach drafts** for sales, based on public information about a prospect's business.

Human role: every claim, testimonial and comparison must be accurate and fair. Never invent reviews or testimonials; that is deceptive and illegal in many markets.

### Conversion: making it easy to say yes

- **Landing page and ad copy variants** for testing.
- **Sales email and follow-up sequences.**
- **Chat assistants** that answer common pre-purchase questions from an approved knowledge base, with a human hand-off.
- **Proposal drafts** from a discovery-call summary.

Human role: price, offer terms and guarantees must match reality exactly. Watch for pressure tactics or false urgency, which consumer-protection regulators treat as misleading.

### Retention: keeping and growing customers

- **Onboarding sequences** and how-to content.
- **Review and feedback analysis:** cluster hundreds of reviews into themes.
- **Win-back and loyalty messages** tailored by segment.
- **Community management:** draft replies to common comments for a human to approve.

Human role: respect opt-outs and consent, and keep a human voice for complaints and sensitive situations.

### Hands-on: map one month of AI use to your funnel

Paste this into your brand project and fill it in with your real channels:

```text
Here is our funnel and current activity:
Awareness: [channels, content, cadence]
Consideration: [website pages, reviews, comparisons, webinars]
Conversion: [checkout, booking, sales calls, offers]
Retention: [email, WhatsApp, loyalty, support]
For each stage, suggest 2 AI uses that would save the most time or improve results,
the human checkpoint each needs, the metric to watch, and one risk (data, claims, disclosure).
Use the lessons from our research file. Return a table.
```

A typical result for a small e-commerce brand (illustrative):

| Stage | AI use | Human checkpoint | Metric |
|---|---|---|---|
| Awareness | Repurpose one weekly video into 5 short assets | Choose points, check claims | Reach, hook retention |
| Consideration | Draft FAQ answers from anonymized customer questions | Accuracy review | Time on page, FAQ clicks |
| Conversion | 4 ad variations per offer across angles | Claims and policy check | Cost per purchase |
| Retention | Personalized win-back email templates with merge fields | Tone and offer approval | Repeat purchase rate |

**Before:** AI is used wherever someone remembers it, mostly for captions.

**After:** two AI uses per stage, each with an owner, a checkpoint and a metric, reviewed monthly.

### Agents and automation across the funnel (what's realistic now)

Assistants with connectors and agent modes can already help with multi-step funnel work: compiling a weekly performance summary from shared reports, drafting personalized follow-ups for approval from CRM notes (in approved tools), or monitoring review sites and summarizing new feedback. Keep humans on anything that publishes, sends to customers, changes budgets or makes claims.

### Measurement across the funnel

AI can also help you interpret results: paste an anonymized performance export and ask for patterns, then verify them in the platform. Treat AI analysis as a hypothesis generator, not the final word.

### A worked example: a UK online tutor

Priya runs GCSE math tutoring online.

- **Awareness:** AI drafts 30 short-video ideas around common exam mistakes; she films her ten favorites.
- **Consideration:** she anonymizes parent WhatsApp questions, has AI cluster them, and turns the top five into an FAQ carousel.
- **Conversion:** AI drafts a three-email sequence for parents who downloaded her free worksheet. She edits for accuracy and adds a real (consented) parent testimonial.
- **Retention:** AI turns her lesson notes into a weekly progress-update template she personalizes for each student.

She measures bookings from each stage and keeps what works.

### Pitfalls to avoid

- Flooding every channel with average AI content. Quality and relevance beat volume.
- Fake social proof, whether invented reviews, AI "customers" or fabricated case studies.
- Personalization that feels creepy because it uses data people did not expect you to have.

lessons.title: Building your first repeatable AI workflow
lessons.body:
### From one-off prompts to workflows

A one-off prompt saves minutes. A repeatable workflow saves hours every week and produces consistent quality. A workflow is simply a documented sequence of steps, some done by AI and some by you, that you run the same way each time.

### The anatomy of a good workflow

1. **Trigger:** what starts it (a new long video is published, a client sends a brief, a week begins).
2. **Inputs:** what you feed in (transcript, brief, brand voice guide, approved claims).
3. **AI steps:** clear prompts saved in your library.
4. **Human checkpoints:** where you review, choose, edit and verify.
5. **Output:** the finished deliverable and where it goes.
6. **Measure:** what you track to know it is working.

### Worked example: the "one video, seven assets" workflow

Faisal is a fitness creator in Jeddah who publishes one long YouTube video a week in Arabic and English.

**Trigger:** the weekly video is uploaded.

**Inputs:** the auto-generated transcript (checked for major errors), his one-page brand voice guide, and a list of topics he never gives advice on (medical conditions, supplements).

**Step 1 (AI): Summarize.** "Here is the transcript of my video. List the five most useful, specific points, in my words where possible. Quote timestamps."

**Step 2 (human): Choose.** Faisal picks the three strongest points.

**Step 3 (AI): Draft.** Using his saved prompt: "Using my brand voice guide below, write: (a) three short-video scripts under 45 seconds, each built around one point with a strong first-line hook; (b) one carousel with 7 slides; (c) one newsletter section of about 200 words; (d) two community posts. Do not add advice beyond what is in the transcript."

**Step 4 (human): Edit and verify.** He checks every fitness claim against what he actually said, removes anything that sounds like medical advice, adds a personal detail, and has his Arabic editor polish the Arabic versions.

**Step 5 (human + tool): Schedule.** Assets go into his scheduler with captions and appropriate disclosures for any sponsored segments.

**Measure:** time spent per week, and views, saves and newsletter clicks for repurposed assets versus before.

Illustratively, if repurposing used to take him most of a working day, a workflow like this might cut it to a couple of hours, with better consistency. Your numbers will differ; measure your own.

### Documenting your workflow

Write it down in a simple template:

| Field | Your answer |
|---|---|
| Name | e.g. Weekly video repurposing |
| Trigger | |
| Inputs | |
| Prompts used (link to library) | |
| Human checkpoints | |
| Output and destination | |
| Quality checklist | |
| Metric | |

Keep prompts in a shared document so a teammate or freelancer can run the workflow too.

### Quality checklist (use for every output)

- Does it sound like us, not like generic AI?
- Is every fact, number and claim verified?
- Is it right for this audience, culture and platform?
- Are disclosures (#ad, paid partnership, AI labels where required) correct?
- Is there any personal or confidential data that should not be there?

### Common pitfalls

- **Automating a bad process.** Fix the process first.
- **Skipping checkpoints** when busy, which is exactly when errors slip through.
- **Never updating prompts.** Review monthly and improve based on what you had to edit.
- **Measuring only volume.** More posts is not the goal; better results for less effort is.

### Hands-on: automate one step (no code)

Once your workflow runs well by hand for a few weeks, automate the **boring, low-risk** steps and keep the human checkpoints:

| Level | Example for the video repurposing workflow |
|---|---|
| **1. Saved prompts + reminder** | A calendar reminder every Monday, prompts saved in the brand project |
| **2. Built-in schedules and agents** | A scheduled task or Notion Custom Agent that collects the week's transcripts into a page and drafts the extraction step |
| **3. Automation platform** | A Zapier or Make scenario: new video published, then fetch transcript, then an AI step drafts the extraction, then save to a review folder and notify you |

A simple Zapier-style recipe (adapt to your tools):

```text
Trigger: New video published on [channel]
Step 1: Get transcript (from your video platform or transcription tool)
Step 2: AI step - prompt: "List the 7 most useful points with timestamps. Flag claims needing a source."
Step 3: Create a document in [Drive/Notion] titled "[date] repurposing - REVIEW"
Step 4: Send me a Slack/email notification with the link
(Nothing is published automatically. Drafting and publishing stay manual.)
```

**Before:** every Monday you remember (or forget) to download the transcript and start from scratch.

**After:** on Monday morning a review document is waiting with the extracted points; you choose, draft in your project and schedule. The automation removed the admin, not your judgment.

### Where to go next

You now have the fundamentals: how AI works, today's assistant features, safe and honest use, and hands-on workflows across the funnel. Next steps:

- [Prompt Engineering for Content & Sales](/learn/prompt-engineering-for-content-and-sales) to sharpen your content and sales prompts.
- [Prompt Engineering Foundations](/learn/prompt-engineering-foundations) for a broader pattern library, then [Advanced Prompt Engineering](/learn/advanced-prompt-engineering) if you build prompts into products.
- [Mastering ChatGPT](/learn/mastering-chatgpt) and [Mastering Claude](/learn/mastering-claude) to go deep on one assistant.
- [AI-Powered Performance Marketing](/learn/ai-performance-marketing) for AI ad platforms, testing and measurement.

scenes.narration: Think of a restaurant recipe card. The head chef doesn't make every plate. They write the recipe down, precisely, and any trained cook in the kitchen can produce the same dish. That's what documenting your workflow does. And just like a recipe, it improves over time. When a dish comes back to the kitchen, the chef adjusts the recipe, not just that one plate. When you find yourself making the same edit to AI drafts every week, update the prompt in the workflow, not just that week's draft.

The recipe card analogy
• Written down
• Same every time
• Anyone in the kitchen can follow it

scenes.narration: Let's walk through a real style example. Faisal is a fitness creator in Jeddah who publishes one long video a week in Arabic and English. Trigger: the weekly video is uploaded. Inputs: the transcript, checked for major errors, his one page brand voice guide, and a list of topics he never gives advice on, like medical conditions and supplements. AI step: list the five most useful points in his words, with timestamps. Human step: he chooses the three strongest. AI step: draft three short scripts, a carousel, a newsletter section and two community posts, and don't add advice beyond the transcript. Human step: he checks every fitness claim, removes anything that sounds like medical advice, and his Arabic editor polishes the Arabic. Then it's scheduled, with disclosures on any sponsored segments.
scenes.onScreen:
Example: Faisal's video workflow
• Trigger: weekly video
• Extract, choose, draft
• Verify, polish, schedule

Timing (57s): title 0-2s; upload and extract steps appear at 10s; choose and draft steps appear at 28s; verify, polish and schedule steps appear at 44s; hold to 57s.

scenes.narration: Notice one instruction in Faisal's workflow: don't add advice beyond the transcript. Why does that matter so much? Because one week, before he added it, a draft script suggested a supplement dose he never mentioned in his video. That's a hallucination, and in fitness it's a potentially harmful one. The model filled a gap with something plausible from its training. Restricting AI steps to your inputs, your transcript, your brief, your approved claims, is the single most effective guardrail in any content workflow. It keeps the content accurate, and it keeps it genuinely yours.
scenes.onScreen:
Why restrict AI to the inputs
• Stops invented advice
• Protects the creator
• Keeps it his voice

scenes.narration: Now write it down. A simple table works: the workflow's name, the trigger, the inputs, links to the prompts in your library or project, the human checkpoints, the output and where it goes, the quality checklist, and the metric. The quality checklist is short. Does it sound like us, not generic AI? Is every fact and claim verified? Is it right for this audience, culture and platform? Are disclosures correct? Is there any personal or confidential data that shouldn't be there? Keep the whole thing in a shared document so a teammate or freelancer can run it on their first day.

Document it
• Name, trigger, inputs
• Prompts, checkpoints, output
• Quality checklist and metric

Timing (44s): title 0-2s; name, trigger and inputs rows fill at 8s; prompts row links to library at 21s; checklist card attaches at 34s; hold to 44s.

scenes.narration: Let me document and automate one. I fill in the table for a weekly podcast repurposing workflow: trigger, new episode; inputs, transcript and voice guide; prompts linked; checkpoints, I choose points and verify claims; output, scheduled posts; metric, time spent and saves per post. Now automation. After running it by hand for a month, I know the boring part: fetching the transcript and running the extraction prompt. In a no code automation tool, I connect four steps. New episode published. Get the transcript. An AI step with my extraction prompt. Create a review document in my drive and send me a notification. That's it. Notice what I didn't automate: choosing, drafting approval, and publishing. On Monday morning, the review document is waiting. The automation removed the admin, not my judgment.
scenes.onScreen:
Watch me do it
• Document the workflow
• Automate one boring step
• Keep publishing manual

Timing (57s): workflow table completed 10s; four automation steps connect 28s; unconnected Publish step shows a lock 44s; hold.

scenes.narration: You don't have to jump straight to automation platforms. Think in three levels. Level one: saved prompts in your project plus a calendar reminder. It sounds basic, but it's the foundation. Level two: built in schedules and agents. A scheduled task in your assistant, or a Notion Custom Agent that runs on a trigger, can collect the week's transcripts into a page and run the extraction prompt for you. Level three: an automation platform like Zapier, Make or n8n, where a trigger in one app kicks off an AI step and then saves or sends the result somewhere else. Most small teams get most of the value from levels one and two. Move up a level only when the workflow is stable and the step you're automating is boring and low risk.

Three levels of automation
• Saved prompts and a reminder
• Scheduled tasks and custom agents
• An automation platform

scenes.narration: The common mistakes. Automating a bad process. Fix the process by hand first, then automate. Skipping checkpoints when you're busy, which is exactly when errors slip through. Never updating prompts. Review them monthly and bake in the edits you keep making. And measuring only volume. More posts isn't the goal. Better results for less effort is. Track time spent and the metric that matters for the channel, like saves, clicks or replies.

keyTakeaways: A workflow has a trigger, inputs, AI steps, human checkpoints, an output and a metric.
Restrict AI steps to your inputs (transcript, brief, approved claims) to avoid invented advice.
Document the workflow so a teammate or freelancer can run it, and review prompts monthly.
Automate boring, low-risk steps first (collecting, extracting, notifying) and keep publishing and claims human.

knowledgeCheck.question: In Faisal's workflow, why does he restrict the AI to what is in the transcript?
options: To save tokens
Because AI cannot write fitness content
To make the output longer
To prevent the AI adding unverified or risky advice he never gave
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Grounding the AI in the transcript reduces hallucinated or risky advice, especially on health topics.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which metric best shows a content workflow is working?
options: Number of posts produced
Time saved alongside engagement or conversion results compared to before
Length of prompts
Number of AI tools used
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Volume alone is not success. Compare time and results before and after the workflow.

lessons.activity: Document one repeatable AI workflow for your own work using the template, run it once this week, and record the time taken and one improvement.

pool.question: What best describes how a large language model produces a caption?
options: It copies the top-ranking caption from the platform
It generates text by repeatedly predicting likely next tokens based on learned patterns
It asks a human writer in real time
It retrieves the best caption from a database of approved posts
pool.explanation: LLMs generate text token by token from learned patterns. They do not retrieve approved posts or copy live content.

pool.question: A friend says, 'AI is basically Google that writes nicely.' What is the most accurate correction?
options: Not quite; many answers come from learned patterns, not live search, so they can be outdated or invented
Not quite; it only works offline
Correct; it searches the web for every answer
Correct; it only shows verified facts
pool.explanation: Unless connected to search or your files, an assistant answers from training patterns, which can be wrong or out of date.

pool.question: You paste a 100-page brochure and after a long session the assistant begins inventing features. What is the BEST fix?
options: Switch the language to English
Keep asking in the same chat until it gets it right
Start a fresh chat, paste only the relevant sections and instruct it to use only the supplied facts
Ask it to be more creative
pool.explanation: Long contexts dilute attention. A fresh chat with focused, grounded input and a 'use only these facts' instruction is the reliable fix.

pool.question: Why can long prompts in Urdu or Arabic hit a tool's limits sooner than similar English prompts?
options: Tools charge extra for non-English words
The context window shrinks for non-English users
Those languages are not supported at all
Text in those scripts often uses more tokens for the same meaning
pool.explanation: Tokenization often splits text in other scripts into more tokens, so limits are reached sooner.

pool.question: Which is the clearest example of an AI hallucination?
options: A caption that is slightly too long
An image with a blue background
A blog draft citing a research report that does not exist
A reply written in a formal tone
pool.explanation: Hallucinations are fluent but false or unsupported content, such as a non-existent report.

pool.question: Which prompt instructions help reduce hallucinated statistics? Select all that apply.
options: 'Do not invent statistics; insert [STAT NEEDED] where one would help'
'Give me as many impressive numbers as possible'
'List any assumptions you made at the end'
'Use only the information in the text below'
pool.explanation: Placeholders, grounding and surfacing assumptions reduce risk. Asking for impressive numbers encourages fabrication.

pool.question: You ask the same factual question twice and get two different numbers. What does this MOST strongly suggest?
options: Your account has been hacked
The model is learning from your chat in real time
Inference is variable and the model lacks a reliable grounded source; verify with a primary source
The second answer is correct because it is newer
pool.explanation: Different answers to the same factual question signal uncertainty. Neither is reliable until checked against an authoritative source.

pool.question: Which statement about training and your chats is most accurate?
options: Every message instantly retrains the model
Chats may or may not be used to improve future models depending on the provider, plan and settings
No provider ever uses chats for training
Only images are used for training
pool.explanation: Models do not learn live from your chat, but providers' policies on using conversations for future training vary by plan and settings.

pool.question: Which task is generally the STRONGEST fit for AI?
options: Turning a video transcript into draft posts for several platforms
Final legal review of an influencer contract
Guaranteeing a headline is exactly 30 characters
Stating the exact current advertising rules in KSA from memory
pool.explanation: Repurposing existing content is a core strength. Legal rules, legal review and exact character counts need verification or professionals.

pool.question: A café's AI-written captions all sound like 'Elevate your coffee experience'. What is the MOST effective fix?
options: Add more emojis
Use a different AI tool
Ask for longer captions
Give the model specifics: real stories, customer phrases, a voice guide and banned phrases
pool.explanation: Generic output comes from lack of specifics. Brand-specific context and banned phrases move output away from the average.

pool.question: When evaluating AI tools for an agency, which criteria belong on the scorecard? Select all that apply.
options: Quality on your own real tasks
Whether inputs are used for training and whether you can opt out
How many followers the founder has
Commercial-use rights for outputs
pool.explanation: Data terms, real-task quality and commercial rights matter. Founder popularity does not predict fitness for your work.

pool.question: What is usually the lowest-friction way to start using AI for design work?
options: Hiring a data scientist
Using AI features built into the design tool you already use
Building your own model
Subscribing to every new tool
pool.explanation: Built-in AI in existing tools fits your current workflow with minimal setup or cost.

pool.question: A Riyadh brand wants a Ramadan campaign. Which split of responsibilities is MOST appropriate?
options: AI decides timing around iftar; humans pick emojis
AI generates concepts and drafts; humans decide cultural fit, final Arabic wording, timing and claims
Humans do everything because AI cannot write Arabic
AI writes and publishes final Arabic copy; humans review metrics later
pool.explanation: AI accelerates ideation and drafting, while cultural sensitivity, final language, timing and claims need human judgment.

pool.question: Why keep your prompt library and brand voice guide in your own documents?
options: It lets you switch tools or onboard teammates without losing your working system
AI tools forbid saving prompts
It makes outputs longer
It prevents hallucinations entirely
pool.explanation: Owning your prompts avoids lock-in and makes workflows shareable. It does not eliminate hallucinations.

pool.question: Which question belongs in a decision checklist before using AI on a task?
options: Is it Friday?
How many tokens is my name?
Which color is the tool's logo?
Is the output easy to check, and what does an error cost?
pool.explanation: Ease of checking and cost of error determine how much review a task needs.

pool.question: Which item should NEVER be pasted into a general AI tool?
options: An anonymized summary of complaint themes
A client's social media login password
A generic question about hooks
A public blog post you wrote
pool.explanation: Credentials are on the red list. Public, generic and anonymized content is low risk.

pool.question: You want AI help analyzing customer complaints from your WhatsApp Business chats. What is the safest approach?
options: Post the chats publicly for feedback
Summarize or anonymize the complaints (themes, no names or numbers), then use an approved tool
Export all chats with phone numbers into a free chatbot
Ask customers to paste their own chats into AI
pool.explanation: Anonymizing and minimizing data before using an approved tool keeps the insight without exposing personal data.

pool.question: Which principles are shared by GDPR-style data protection laws in many regions? Select all that apply.
options: Use data only for the stated purpose
Share data freely once it is online
Collect only the data you need
Keep data secure
pool.explanation: Data minimization, purpose limitation and security are common principles. Online availability does not remove protection.

pool.question: An agency's clinic client sends patient enquiries for social content ideas. What is the BEST practice?
options: Manually extract anonymized themes (e.g. 'questions about appointment times') and never input patient details into AI
Store enquiries in a personal AI chat for later
Paste enquiries into AI so it can find patterns
Use patient names in posts to add authenticity
pool.explanation: Health data is highly sensitive. Extract anonymized themes manually and keep identifiable patient information out of AI tools.

pool.question: What is the most useful first step to reduce data risk in a tool you already use?
options: Turn on notifications
Change its theme to dark mode
Check its training, retention and memory settings
Increase your prompt length
pool.explanation: Reviewing training opt-outs, retention and memory settings directly reduces how your data is stored and used.

pool.question: Which proposal clause about AI is most appropriate for a small agency?
options: 'We do not disclose tool use under any circumstances'
'We use approved AI tools, review all outputs, avoid putting confidential information into tools that train on it, and require written consent for any likeness or voice'
'AI is responsible for all errors'
'We may use any AI tool with any data you provide'
pool.explanation: Transparent commitments on approved tools, review, data and consent set clear, trustworthy expectations.

pool.question: A teammate pasted a client's unreleased pricing into a personal free chatbot. Which steps are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Assess whether the client must be informed under the contract
Delete the chat and check the tool's data settings
Report it to the account lead
Hide the incident so the client never finds out
pool.explanation: A transparent incident process limits harm and respects contractual duties. Hiding it increases legal and trust risk.

pool.question: Generating 20 short-video ideas to reach new audiences mainly supports which funnel stage?
options: Retention
Consideration
Awareness
Conversion
pool.explanation: Discovery content that reaches new people is awareness.

pool.question: Which AI use is most appropriate for the retention stage?
options: Buying followers
Clustering existing customer reviews into themes to improve onboarding
Cold outreach to new prospects
Writing hooks for first-time viewers
pool.explanation: Retention focuses on existing customers; review analysis and onboarding improvements serve that stage.

pool.question: An AI-drafted sales email says 'Only 2 spots left, offer ends tonight!' but neither is true. What is the correct action?
options: Send it only to international customers
Send it; urgency increases conversions
Soften it to 'probably ends tonight'
Remove or correct the false urgency, because misleading scarcity claims can breach consumer-protection rules
pool.explanation: False urgency and scarcity are misleading practices in many markets. Offer terms must match reality.

pool.question: Which elements belong in a documented AI workflow? Select all that apply.
options: Saved prompts
A promise that no editing is needed
A trigger that starts it
Human review checkpoints
pool.explanation: Triggers, prompts and human checkpoints define a repeatable workflow. No responsible workflow skips editing.

pool.question: What is the best way to judge whether an AI content workflow is working?
options: Count how many AI tools are involved
Compare time spent and results such as saves, clicks or bookings before and after
Ask the AI if it is working
Count how many posts it produces
pool.explanation: Effectiveness is time saved plus results, measured against a baseline.

pool.question: A fitness creator's AI-drafted short script suggests a supplement dose never mentioned in his video. What does this reveal about his workflow?
options: Supplement advice is always safe
The AI is helping by adding value
He should stop making videos
The prompt should restrict the AI to transcript content and his checkpoint must catch unapproved health advice
pool.explanation: Grounding plus a human verification checkpoint prevents risky, unsourced health advice.

pool.question: A tutor wants to personalize parent emails using AI. Which approach balances effectiveness and trust?
options: Use information parents knowingly shared (child's level, goals) and respect opt-outs
Let AI send emails automatically without review
Scrape parents' social media to infer income and target offers
Send identical emails to everyone forever
pool.explanation: Personalization using expected, consented data with opt-outs respected builds trust; inferring sensitive traits from scraped data feels invasive and may be unlawful.

pool.question: Which statements about the context window are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: It permanently stores all your past conversations
It limits how much text the model can consider at once
Relevant documents must be supplied for the model to use them
Pasting irrelevant material can distract the model
pool.explanation: The context window is working memory for the current interaction, not permanent storage. Relevant, focused context gives better results.

pool.question: An owner wants AI to 'decide our pricing strategy'. What is the most appropriate use of AI here?
options: Let AI set prices based on general knowledge
Use AI to structure the analysis and draft questions, while decisions rest on the owner's own cost, demand and competitor data
Avoid AI completely for any business thinking
Copy competitor prices suggested by AI without checking
pool.explanation: AI helps structure thinking but gives average advice without your data. Decisions need your specific numbers and judgment.

pool.question: Which is an appropriate AI use in the consideration stage?
options: Creating fake reviewer accounts
Inventing testimonials
Hiding prices
Drafting an honest comparison of your two service packages
pool.explanation: Honest explainers and comparisons help people evaluate you. Fabricated social proof is deceptive.

pool.question: A marketer manages three client brands. What is the best way to keep each brand's voice guide, approved claims and product sheets available to the assistant without mixing them?
options: Put all three in global custom instructions
Create one project per brand with its own instructions and files
Tell the assistant's memory about each brand
Paste everything into every chat
pool.explanation: Projects keep brand-specific instructions and files together and separate. Global instructions and memory apply everywhere, so client details can leak across brands.

pool.question: Which uses match the right assistant feature? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Deep research for a cited competitor positioning report
File analysis to find themes in 300 anonymized reviews
Voice mode to rehearse a pitch with a skeptical buyer
A temporary chat to store your brand kit permanently
pool.explanation: Deep research, file analysis and voice fit those jobs. Temporary chats aren't saved or used for memory, so they can't hold a brand kit.

pool.question: An influencer's sponsored video was scripted with AI help. Which disclosure is required?
options: An AI label only
The platform's paid partnership label and #ad (or local equivalent)
No disclosure, because AI wrote the script
A disclosure in the video description only if asked
pool.explanation: Advertising disclosure depends on the paid relationship. An AI-assisted script doesn't need an AI label; realistic synthetic media would.

pool.question: A brand wants AI-generated 'real customers' praising a product in ads, with a small 'AI-generated' label. What's the best advice?
options: Fine, because it's labeled
Don't present AI-generated people as real customers or testimonials; a label doesn't cure a misleading impression
Fine if the product is popular
Fine outside the EU
pool.explanation: Fake testimonials are prohibited (for example under the FTC rule on fake reviews and testimonials) and misleading under advertising codes; disclosure doesn't fix a false claim.

pool.question: Before creating a synthetic voice of your agency's founder for ads, what do you need?
options: Nothing, if the tool allows it
The founder's explicit written consent and an agreed scope of use
A platform AI label only
A higher subscription tier
pool.explanation: Synthetic voices and likenesses of real people require explicit, documented consent.

pool.question: Which input gives you customer language that competitors don't have?
options: A deep research report on the industry
Your own anonymized reviews, survey answers and support messages
A generic persona template
Stock photos
pool.explanation: Voice-of-customer mining on your own data surfaces unique, verbatim phrases for hooks and headlines.

pool.question: An AI draft produces three personas. What is the right next step?
options: Build the whole strategy on them
Treat them as hypotheses and validate them with a few customer conversations, a poll or analytics
Delete them; AI personas are useless
Add stock photos and publish them
pool.explanation: AI personas are useful starting points but must be validated before they guide strategy.

pool.question: Why should a creative brief have a single-minded message?
options: It is shorter to write
One clear idea gives creative work focus; several ideas usually produce cluttered work that says nothing
Platforms require it
AI can only process one idea
pool.explanation: A single-minded message is the core of a strong brief for human and AI creators alike.

pool.question: You ask AI to draft a brief from your call notes. Which instructions improve it? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Use only facts from my notes
Write [DECIDE] where my notes are silent
Invent a budget if none is given
Then critique it as a demanding creative director
pool.explanation: Grounding, explicit placeholders and a stress test improve briefs; inventing a budget creates a false decision.

pool.question: A team plans to publish 300 AI-generated location pages with near-identical text to rank for every city. What's the main risk?
options: Pages will load slowly
Mass-produced low-value pages can violate search spam policies (scaled content abuse) and won't help users
Search engines can't read AI text
It uses too many tokens
pool.explanation: Search guidance judges helpfulness however content is made; scaled thin pages risk spam policies.

pool.question: In a repurposing chain, what should the AI drafts be restricted to?
options: Anything trending this week
The points you chose from the source, with no added advice or facts
Competitors' content
General knowledge about the topic
pool.explanation: Restricting drafts to the chosen source points keeps content accurate and yours.

pool.question: You ask for 10 ad variations and get 10 rewordings of the same idea. What's the fix?
options: Ask for 50 variations
Ask for variations across distinct angles (pain, desire, social proof, curiosity, objection) and label each
Use more emojis
Remove the offer
pool.explanation: Distinct angles make tests informative; near-identical wording teaches you little.

pool.question: An AI table says all 15 of your Google Ads headlines are within the character limit. What should you do?
options: Trust it and upload
Verify counts yourself with a counter, because models can miscount characters
Shorten every headline by half
Ask the AI again until it agrees
pool.explanation: Models process tokens, not letters, so character counts need independent checking.

pool.question: What should you do FIRST with a new 90-day campaign export before asking analysis questions?
options: Build charts
Inspect it: date range, totals, missing values, duplicates and odd entries
Share it with the client
Delete old rows
pool.explanation: Inspection catches problems like duplicated weeks before they distort conclusions.

pool.question: Your AI summary adds Meta, Google Ads and email conversions to report 'total sales'. The total is higher than actual orders. Why?
options: The AI made an arithmetic error
Platforms use different attribution rules and count overlapping conversions
Email tools don't report conversions
Orders are always undercounted
pool.explanation: Platform-reported conversions overlap and use different windows; compare against your own sales data.

pool.question: You want to automate part of a weekly repurposing workflow. Which step is the best first candidate?
options: Publishing posts automatically
Fetching the transcript and running the extraction prompt into a review document
Approving claims
Replying to comments automatically
pool.explanation: Automate boring, low-risk admin first; keep choosing, claim checks and publishing human.
